strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored evaluation gap: 3D spatial geometric consistency in generated videos, clearly distinguishing it from fidelity metrics (FVD) and 2D consistency metrics (VBench, MEt3R).

Proposes a physically grounded diagnostic metric based on the principle that static background points should share a single camera transformation; the multi-component design (local/global pose consistency, depth consistency) gives interpretable failure modes rather than a single opaque score.

Provides extensive empirical validation: 1,296 videos, 10 generative models, 3 real-world anchors, several baselines, controlled synthetic perturbations with monotonicity checks, motion-stratified analysis, and ablations.
Well written and generally clear; the pipeline, hyperparameters, algorithm boxes, and appendix details support understanding and at least partial reproducibility.
Demonstrates that SGC can diverge from FVD/VBench and identify failures missed by 2D metrics, supporting its value as a complementary diagnostic tool.
weaknesses: The core metric depends on off-the-shelf geometry models (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo), but the paper does not analyze sensitivity to depth/pose/tracking errors. More critically, replacing VGGT depth with Video Depth Anything may introduce unaddressed depth-scale ambiguity: VDA depth is not guaranteed to be scale-consistent with VGGT camera translations/intrinsics, yet global translational variance and depth consistency compare quantities across these sources without describing scale alignment.

The PCA-based aggregation weights and dataset-level normalization are learned on the full 1,296-video evaluation/calibration set, and the final benchmark scores use these fitted weights. Although a 10-fold stability check is reported, this is still calibration on the test set; held-out or fixed aggregation would make the benchmark claims stronger.

There is no human perceptual validation or independent ground-truth annotation confirming that SGC rankings match perceived 3D geometric consistency. Controlled synthetic perturbations and real-video anchors are useful but do not fully establish validity for naturally generated failures.

The metric assumes a single rigid static background and sufficient static features. It does not discuss failure cases where the background is non-rigid (water, foliage, smoke, crowds, reflections), where MOS/depth/tracking fails, or where there is too little static background for reliable PnP.

Ablations show the full model is not uniformly best: e.g., Depth+Spatial is better on RT-1 and OpenVid, and w/o MOS is better for Cosmos. MOS can also introduce boundary noise in low-dynamic scenes. These domain-dependent effects are only partially explained.

Local sub-regions are formed by 1D depth clustering rather than spatial coherence; the authors acknowledge that this can merge disjoint surfaces. This weakens the claimed 'spatially coherent sub-region' interpretation and makes local pose variance less directly tied to distinct 3D surfaces.

No runtime, memory, or scalability analysis is provided despite using several heavy pretrained models per video, which matters for adoption as an evaluation benchmark. The code link is blank/absent, limiting reproducibility of the exact implementation.

Dataset accounting is somewhat unclear: the paper states 1,196 GenWorld videos plus 100 OpenVidHD videos but later reports 996 AI-generated videos and 300 real videos, leaving the composition of the remaining videos and their selection criteria insufficiently specified.

Table 1 reports only aggregate scores without uncertainty estimates or significance tests; some differences between methods may be small and should be supported by per-video distributions and statistical comparison.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: evaluating 3D spatial geometric consistency in generated videos, disentangling static background stability from valid foreground motion.
Proposes a physically motivated multi-component metric based on divergence among local camera poses, global pose consistency, and depth consistency.
Provides a relatively comprehensive benchmark with 1,296 videos, 10 generative models, three real-world anchors, multiple baselines, controlled synthetic perturbations, and ablations.
Includes useful analyses such as sensitivity to motion-segmentation quality and PCA weight stability across folds.
Demonstrates qualitatively and quantitatively that SGC can separate real videos from generated ones and can expose failures missed by FVD/VBench-style metrics.
weaknesses: No human evaluation or ground-truth geometric annotation for generated videos is provided. Validation relies mainly on synthetic perturbations and real-vs-generated separation, so it is unclear whether SGC aligns with perceptual 3D consistency.

Methodological circularity: the PCA weights and dataset-level normalization parameters (Z-score/min-max bounds) are learned on the full evaluation dataset and then used to score the same videos. The appendix cross-validation checks weight stability, not held-out generalization, so benchmark fairness remains questionable.

The metric depends heavily on off-the-shelf estimators (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo). Errors or domain shifts in these models on generated videos can be misattributed to the video generator, and no end-to-end validation isolates this confound.

Potential scale ambiguity is not addressed. Local PnP uses depth (likely relative/scale-ambiguous) while global pose comparison relies on VGGT translations; if depth and global pose scales differ, translation-variance and global-consistency components may be invalid.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: SGC benefits from strong 3D foundation models, whereas MEt3R(+MOS) and other baselines use different estimators or masking protocols. This makes it difficult to attribute gains to the metric design rather than the chosen backbones.

The static-background assumption ignores non-rigid background elements (water, foliage, smoke, deformable objects) not captured by moving-object segmentation, which may cause valid dynamic scenes to be penalized.

Ablation results show the full model can be worse than the no-MOS variant on static scenes (e.g., OpenVid: 0.053 vs. 0.014), indicating segmentation noise or mask leakage can degrade the metric without a fully convincing remedy.

The aggregate score is difficult to interpret: two translation components correlate at r≈0.992, so PCA may overweight redundant signals, and the final SGC value depends on dataset-level calibration rather than an absolute per-video scale.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the mentioned code link/availability is not visible, and important implementation choices such as rotation averaging, depth-scale alignment, and exact normalization pipeline are not fully specified.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored evaluation gap: measuring 3D spatial geometric consistency in dynamically generated videos, distinct from fidelity-centric and 2D-consistency metrics.
Proposes a physically grounded metric that isolates static background regions and measures divergence among local camera pose estimates, avoiding penalties for valid foreground motion.
Comprehensive empirical study: 1,296 videos, 10 generative models, three real-world anchors, multiple baselines, controlled synthetic perturbations, ablations, and robustness analyses.
Controlled perturbation experiments show monotonic SGC response to geometric corruption, and component-level perturbations align with intended failure modes, supporting construct validity.
Ablations of moving-object segmentation and depth clustering provide useful insight into design choices, especially the importance of isolating dynamic foregrounds.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and provides substantial implementation details and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf modules (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo) as black boxes; failure modes of these estimators on generated videos are not analyzed. In particular, VGGT global poses are estimated from full frames without masking dynamic objects, so foreground motion may confound the global reference pose.

Depth scale alignment is not specified: Video Depth Anything may output relative/affine-invariant depth, while PnP-based local pose estimation and depth-consistency warping require depths to be metrically aligned with VGGT intrinsics/camera poses. If scale alignment is missing, translational variance and depth-consistency terms may be ill-posed.

SGC is dataset-level normalized: PCA weights and Z-score/min-max calibration are learned on the same 1,296-video evaluation set. This limits SGC as a per-video absolute metric and raises concerns about generalization to new models or datasets; internal cross-validation does not fully address external calibration dependence.

No human perceptual study or exact 3D/camera ground truth for generated videos is provided. Validity is supported mainly by synthetic perturbations and real-vs-generated separation, but it is not established that SGC rankings align with human judgments of 3D geometric consistency.

Motion disentanglement is not fully resolved: generated models still show substantial SGC-ECD correlations (e.g., Latte r=0.79), so residual motion sensitivity or estimator noise may contribute to SGC scores. The claim of robustness to camera motion is supported but not definitively proven.

Several methodological details are underspecified or missing in the main paper: the local translational variance formula, scale handling, invalid-depth treatment, minimum track/subregion constraints, and exactly how dataset-level normalization parameters are applied in the reported benchmark comparison.

Baseline adaptations such as MEt3R(+MOS) and PCA-weighted VBench composite may alter baseline behavior; while intended for fairness, they make the comparison less standard. A comparison to a ground-truth camera-consistency metric on synthetic data with known geometry would strengthen validation.

strengths: Addresses an important evaluation gap: existing fidelity metrics are insensitive to 3D geometric distortions, while consistency metrics are confounded by valid foreground motion. The proposed SGC targets static-background geometric stability with a clear, physically grounded principle.

The pipeline is reasonably well motivated and modular: static/dynamic separation, depth-based sub-region partitioning, local PnP pose estimation, and aggregation of inter-segment, global, and depth consistency terms.

The empirical study is extensive, covering 10 generative models across T2V/I2V/V2V, multiple real-world anchors, several baselines, controlled synthetic perturbations, ablations, estimator-robustness checks, and a human study.
The controlled perturbation experiments provide useful evidence that SGC responds monotonically to geometric degradation, supporting its construct validity beyond simple texture or semantics.
Component analyses, PCA weight cross-validation, motion-stratified distributions, and MOS sensitivity analyses make the metric design and failure modes reasonably transparent.
The human study reports strong alignment with human judgments of static-background 3D stability, which is important for an evaluation metric paper.
weaknesses: A potentially serious technical issue is the reliance on two different geometry sources without clearly addressing scale alignment: VGGT is used for global poses/intrinsics, while Video Depth Anything is used for depth. If the depth is relative or scale-invariant, PnP translation estimates and comparisons against VGGT global translations may be scale-inconsistent, especially because translation-related terms dominate the PCA weights.

The final SGC score is dataset-normalized and uses PCA weights learned on the full evaluation set. This prevents SGC from functioning as an absolute, standalone metric and makes comparisons across datasets or on single videos difficult; it also risks subtle test-set leakage through dataset-level normalization statistics.

Static-background isolation via motion segmentation may remove exactly the regions where geometric inconsistency manifests, especially if failures cause static structures to be classified as dynamic. This creates a potential blind spot and some tension with the paper's motivating failure cases (e.g., object impermanence).

The metric's robustness to camera motion is only partially demonstrated. On some generated videos the correlation between motion and SGC is high (e.g., Latte r≈0.79), so valid high motion may still be penalized due to tracking/depth failures rather than genuine geometric inconsistency.

The technical novelty is limited: the method largely integrates existing foundation models (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo) with PnP and PCA aggregation. The contribution is mainly a metric/pipeline rather than a new geometric algorithm.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code or data release is mentioned, and several implementation details are missing, including depth-scale alignment, mask propagation across frames, PnP failure handling, and how normalization statistics are fixed for new videos.

Baseline comparisons are not uniformly adapted. MEt3R gets a motion-segmented variant, but other baselines operate under different assumptions; the VBench weighted composite is also recalibrated on the same dataset, which complicates claims of fair unified comparison.
The human study is useful but relatively small (7 annotators, 150 pairs, 11 aggregated entities), so the reported high correlation should be interpreted with caution.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: 3D spatial geometric consistency in dynamically generated videos, which is not well captured by FVD, VBench, or 2D feature-consistency metrics.
Proposes a physically grounded metric that explicitly isolates static background regions before estimating local camera poses, thereby attempting to avoid penalizing valid foreground motion.
Provides a fairly extensive empirical study: 1,296 videos across real and generated sources, multiple baselines, component ablations, controlled synthetic perturbations, and an appendix human study.

The controlled perturbation experiments demonstrate monotonic sensitivity to geometric corruptions, and the ranking-stability analysis across different geometry estimators is useful evidence that the metric is not purely an artifact of one backbone.
The paper is generally well organized and includes implementation details, hyperparameters, and additional qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The metric is calibrated using PCA weights and normalization statistics computed on the full evaluation dataset, including the videos being evaluated. This is a form of test-set leakage and makes the reported SGC scores benchmark-specific rather than independent measurements. The cross-validation in Appendix D.1 only validates weight stability, not that the main evaluation avoids calibration leakage.

No fixed normalization parameters (means, standard deviations, min/max bounds) are provided for reproducing the SGC scores. Because Z-score and min-max normalization are dataset-level operations, the metric cannot be applied to a single new video or a new dataset without recalibrating on a reference set, which undermines its practical use as a standalone metric.

The pipeline depends on multiple off-the-shelf estimators (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo) that were not designed for generative video artifacts. In particular, there is no clear handling of depth scale/shift inconsistency between frames or between local sub-regions, which can directly corrupt PnP pose estimates and the depth consistency error.

Global camera pose is obtained from VGGT on full frames, while the method's central premise is that geometry should be assessed from static regions only. If dynamic foreground objects corrupt the global pose, the global consistency component may not reflect true background geometry.

The depth-based partitioning is described as producing 'spatially coherent sub-regions,' but the actual implementation clusters only by 1D depth magnitude and can merge disjoint surfaces. The paper acknowledges this but does not resolve the mismatch between the claimed spatial coherence and the method.

Ablations show that removing motion segmentation can improve SGC on static-camera datasets such as OpenVid, and that MOS quality strongly affects scores. This means the metric's behavior is highly dependent on a preprocessing stage that is itself imperfect for generated videos.

The baseline comparison modifies VBench via dataset-specific PCA weighting, which may not represent VBench as originally intended. More importantly, the paper compares mainly against 2D and holistic metrics; it does not compare against other recent 3D/4D geometry-focused evaluation approaches that could strengthen the case for SGC's necessity.

The human study in Appendix E is small (150 pairs, 7 annotators, 11 entity-level points for correlation), and its correlation estimates are likely unstable. While it supports the claim, it is not sufficient on its own to validate the metric across the broader space of generated videos.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: evaluating 3D geometric consistency in generated videos, where existing fidelity-centric metrics (e.g., FVD) are insensitive to geometric distortions and existing consistency metrics (e.g., MEt3R, VBench) are confounded by valid foreground motion.

Physically motivated formulation: static background points should adhere to a single rigid camera transformation, and divergence among local pose estimates provides a principled, interpretable signal for geometric inconsistency.

Well-designed pipeline: static background isolation via MOS, depth-based subregion partitioning, local relative pose estimation via PnP, and global/depth consistency terms; the final PCA-based aggregation avoids subjective manual weighting.

Extensive empirical validation: 10 generative models across T2V, I2V, and V2V paradigms, three real-world anchors (nuScenes, RT-1, OpenVid), multiple baselines, controlled synthetic perturbations, component ablations, estimator robustness checks, and a blinded human study.

Strong evidence of metric validity: SGC exhibits strict monotonic response to geometric perturbations, high agreement with human judgments of static-background stability (Spearman ρ = 0.945), stable rankings across different geometric estimators, and remains robust to camera motion magnitude.
Clear presentation: the paper carefully defines its scope, provides algorithmic details and hyperparameters, and acknowledges limitations and reproducibility considerations.
weaknesses: The metric relies on off-the-shelf estimators (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA, SegAnyMo), so SGC can be affected by estimator domain shift, tracking failures, or segmentation errors. Although the authors test rank stability across backbones, SGC lacks absolute calibration and may partly measure estimator noise during severe generation failures.

Scope is limited to static background geometry: dynamic foreground objects and non-rigid motion are explicitly masked out. This means SGC does not fully evaluate 3D consistency in dynamic video generation; it is a complementary diagnostic rather than a complete metric for all geometric failure modes.

PCA-derived weights and dataset-level Z-score/min-max normalization make the final SGC score relative to the calibration dataset and benchmark composition; cross-validation is reassuring but does not eliminate this dependence.

The custom benchmark and main-text dataset count should be clarified: the paper mentions 1,196 GenWorld videos and 100 web videos, while the table/appendix indicate 996 generative videos plus 300 real videos. Resolution, length, and domain differences between real anchors and generated videos may also affect comparability.

The final composite score is somewhat opaque because it aggregates multiple components via PCA, and the high correlation between local and global translational variance suggests some redundancy among components. Component-level analysis mitigates but does not fully resolve this interpretability concern.
